# Optimizing Compiler Internals: A Technical Brief

## 1. SSA Construction

**Cytron et al. dominance-frontier algorithm.** The canonical construction (Cytron, Ferrante, Rosen, Wegman, Zadeck 1991) builds the dominator tree, computes each node's **dominance frontier** (the set of nodes where a definition's influence stops dominating but is still reachable), and places φ-nodes at the dominance frontier of every definition site, iterating until a fixed point (the "iterated dominance frontier," DF⁺). Variables are then renamed by a dominator-tree walk, pushing a fresh SSA name per definition onto a per-variable stack and popping on exit from a subtree. This produces **minimal SSA** (every live φ is necessary) but not necessarily **pruned SSA** — φ-nodes may be inserted for variables not actually live at that point, hence the common follow-up step of **pruned SSA construction**, which uses liveness information to suppress dead φ-nodes.

**Braun et al. simple construction.** An alternative avoiding explicit dominance-frontier computation: process the CFG in reverse postorder, and when a variable is read in a block, recursively resolve its value — if the block has one predecessor, recurse into it; if multiple, insert a φ and recursively fill its operands, memoizing to handle loops (incomplete φs are marked and completed once all predecessors are known). This is simpler to implement incrementally (useful in JIT front-ends building SSA directly from an AST) and naturally produces a form close to pruned SSA, at the cost of needing a separate **trivial-φ removal** pass to collapse redundant φs where all operands are identical.

**Sreedhar-Gao DJ-graph construction.** Augments the dominator tree (D-edges) with join edges (J-edges) from the CFG to compute dominance frontiers more efficiently without recomputing them from scratch, giving an almost-linear algorithm; it's the basis for several production-compiler SSA builders because it avoids the worst-case quadratic blowup of naive dominance-frontier computation on CFGs with wide fan-in.

**SSA destruction.** Converting back to non-SSA form requires replacing φ-nodes with explicit copies. Naively inserting copies for each φ operand at the end of each predecessor block introduces the **lost-copy problem** (a value is overwritten before a later use due to control-flow ordering) and the **swap problem** (two variables need their values exchanged, which a sequence of copies cannot express without a temporary). Correct destruction algorithms compute an **interference graph among SSA names sharing a φ-web** and use coalescing (e.g. the Sreedhar et al. three-phase algorithm, or Boissinot et al.'s approach using value interference plus a dominance-based coalescing test) to merge SSA names into real variables while provably avoiding both pathologies.

## 2. Alias Analysis

**Andersen's inclusion-based (subset) analysis.** Models each pointer-valued variable as a set of abstract locations it may point to, and generates subset constraints of the form `pts(a) ⊇ pts(b)` from assignments; solving is iterative constraint propagation to a fixed point, equivalent to context-free-language reachability over a constraint graph. It's flow-insensitive but highly precise relative to unification-based methods, with worst-case cubic time in the number of variables — the dominant cost center in whole-program points-to analysis for large C/C++ codebases.

**Steensgaard's unification-based analysis.** Instead of subset constraints, each assignment `a = b` unifies the points-to sets of `a` and `b` using a union-find structure, giving near-linear time at the cost of precision (every alias relationship observed anywhere forces merging, so the result is a much coarser over-approximation). It's the standard choice when speed dominates precision, e.g. in some LTO pipelines.

**Type-based alias analysis (TBAA).** Assumes/exploits a language's type system (e.g. C/C++ strict aliasing rules) to conclude that accesses through pointers of incompatible types cannot alias, independent of points-to computation. LLVM implements this via `!tbaa` metadata attached to loads/stores, encoding a type hierarchy so the optimizer can quickly rule out aliasing between, say, an `int*` and a `struct Foo*` access without running a full points-to analysis — cheap, syntactic, but unsound in the presence of `reinterpret_cast`/`memcpy`-style type punning, which is why `-fno-strict-aliasing` disables it.

**Flow/field/context sensitivity axes.** Flow-sensitive analysis tracks points-to sets per program point (precise, expensive); flow-insensitive computes one set per variable valid everywhere (cheap, standard for whole-program). Field-sensitive analysis distinguishes `obj.f1` from `obj.f2` as separate abstract locations rather than collapsing a whole struct/object to one location (field-insensitive). Context sensitivity (e.g. k-CFA-style call-string distinction, or Andersen variants with context cloning) distinguishes different call sites of the same function so points-to facts aren't polluted across unrelated calls. Must-alias (two expressions are guaranteed to reference the same location on every path) is strictly stronger and much harder to establish than may-alias (they could reference the same location), and compilers mostly compute conservative may-alias information to guard transformations, with must-alias reserved for enabling optimizations like store-to-load forwarding.

**Memory SSA.** Rather than tracking each memory location, a single abstract "heap" value is versioned SSA-style at each store/clobbering call, with loads selecting the nearest dominating memory definition (used in LLVM's `MemorySSA` and GCC's virtual operands); this lets scalar-optimization machinery (dead store elimination, redundancy elimination) operate over memory effects using the same renaming and φ-placement machinery as SSA for registers.

## 3. Register Allocation

**Chaitin-Briggs graph coloring.** Build an **interference graph** where nodes are live ranges and edges connect ranges simultaneously live; a k-coloring (k = number of physical registers) is a valid allocation. The algorithm repeatedly removes ("simplifies") nodes of degree < k onto a stack (such nodes are colorable regardless of neighbors), and when stuck, picks a spill candidate by a cost heuristic (typically *uses+defs weighted by loop depth, divided by degree*) to remove optimistically rather than immediately spilling. Chaitin's original formulation spills immediately upon getting stuck; **Briggs' optimistic coloring** instead pushes the high-degree node onto the stack anyway and defers the spill decision — when popping and assigning colors, it often turns out a color is still free because not all neighbors received distinct colors, substantially reducing unnecessary spills.

**Iterated register coalescing (George-Appel).** Interleaves graph simplification with **coalescing** (merging two live ranges connected by a copy instruction into one node, eliminating the copy) but must avoid coalescing that creates an uncolorable node. **Conservative coalescing** (Briggs' rule: merge only if the combined node has fewer than k neighbors of significant degree) and the **Briggs test**/**George test** are the standard safety checks; coalescing is iterated with simplification/spilling until no more progress is possible, maximizing copy elimination without compromising colorability.

**Linear scan register allocation.** Computes **live intervals** (one contiguous range per variable, an approximation of true liveness) via a single linear-order pass, then sweeps intervals in start-point order maintaining an active set; when the active set exceeds k, evicts (spills) the interval with the furthest-away next use (Poletto-Sarkar's heuristic). It sacrifices some precision relative to graph coloring (intervals, not full interference graphs, can overestimate conflicts) but runs in near-linear time, which is why it's the dominant allocator in JIT compilers (HotSpot's client/C1 compiler, early LLVM "fast" allocator) where compile-time budget is tight.

**SSA-based / chordal graph-coloring allocation.** Because interference graphs of programs in SSA form are provably **chordal** (every live range's definition dominates all its uses), they can be colored optimally in polynomial time via a simplicial elimination ordering, without the NP-hard general graph-coloring heuristics — this is the basis of SSA-based allocators (Hack, Grund, Goos) that solve allocation as a sequence of local "register puzzle" problems per basic block and a global coalescing step, giving provably-good results without Chaitin-Briggs' optimistic-spill guesswork.

## 4. Inlining

**Bottom-up SCC-ordered inlining.** The call graph is condensed into **strongly connected components** (to handle recursion) and processed bottom-up: callees are optimized and have their cost/size finalized before being considered for inlining into callers, so cost estimates reflect the callee's actual optimized body rather than its pre-optimization size. This ordering is standard in GCC and LLVM's inliner pass, which walks the SCC DAG from leaves to roots (with recursive SCCs handled by a fixed iteration/depth cutoff).

**Cost-benefit heuristic models.** LLVM's `InlineCost` analysis walks the callee's IR estimating a size cost (instruction count weighted by predicted simplification — e.g. a branch on a constant argument is assumed to fold away, reducing effective cost) against a threshold that varies by call-site attributes (`hot` callsites via profile data get larger thresholds; always-inline/never-inline attributes short-circuit the heuristic). This is fundamentally a *speculative* cost model: it tries to predict post-inlining simplification (constant folding, dead branch elimination) without actually performing it, trading accuracy for not having to try-and-revert every candidate.

**Recursive inlining limits.** Direct or mutual recursion cannot be fully inlined, so compilers bound inlining depth/size growth with a recursion-count threshold or total-size budget per root function, often combined with **partial inlining** (duplicating only the fast-path prologue of a callee — e.g. a null-check guard — at the call site while leaving the full body as a real call for the slow path), which captures most of the benefit of inlining hot/short paths without the code-size blowup of inlining an entire large recursive or rarely-executed function body.

**Speculative devirtualization + inlining.** When a virtual/indirect call's target can't be statically resolved but profiling or class-hierarchy analysis suggests a dominant likely target, the compiler inserts a runtime type/pointer check guarding an inlined copy of that likely target, with a fallback indirect call otherwise — this converts an otherwise un-inlinable call site into an inlining opportunity, and is a key technique in JIT compilers (V8, HotSpot's C2) working with dynamically-typed or polymorphic call sites.

**Interaction with other passes.** Inlining is widely treated as an *enabling* transformation rather than valuable per se: by exposing a callee's body with actual argument values substituted in, it creates new opportunities for constant propagation, dead-code elimination, and — critically — escape analysis, since a call that previously caused an argument to "escape" into an opaque function may, once inlined, provably not let the object escape at all, enabling stack allocation or scalar replacement that was impossible across the call boundary. This is why inlining decisions are often made conservatively, accepting local size cost, to unlock larger downstream wins.

## 5. Escape Analysis

**Connection-graph analysis (Choi-Gupta-Midkiff).** Builds a graph per method where nodes represent objects (by allocation site) and variables, with edges representing points-to and field-reference relationships; propagating this graph across the call graph classifies each allocation as `NoEscape` (never visible outside the allocating method/thread), `ArgEscape` (passed to a callee but not stored globally or returned), or `GlobalEscape` (reachable after the method returns, e.g. stored into a static field or returned). This classification, used in HotSpot's C2 compiler, directly drives both stack allocation and lock elision decisions.

**Scalar replacement of aggregates (SRA).** Once escape analysis proves an object never escapes, the compiler can replace the heap-allocated object entirely with its constituent scalar fields held in registers/SSA values — no object header, no memory traffic, and the fields become ordinary optimizable SSA variables subject to further constant propagation and dead-field elimination. This is one of the highest-value payoffs of escape analysis because it doesn't just avoid an allocation, it exposes the object's internals to the full scalar optimizer.

**Thread-escape analysis and lock elision.** A narrower variant asks not "does this object escape the method" but "does this object become visible to another thread." If a lock's associated object is proven thread-local, the `monitorenter`/`monitorexit` (or equivalent mutex) pair is redundant and can be elided entirely (biased/lock elision in HotSpot), since no other thread can ever contend for it — this is a correctness-preserving optimization that depends entirely on escape analysis precision, since a false "doesn't escape" conclusion would introduce a data race.

**Partial escape analysis.** Rather than a binary escape/no-escape classification per allocation, Graal's partial escape analysis tracks escape state **per control-flow path** within a method: an object may be provably non-escaping along a fast path (and thus scalar-replaced there) while escaping along a rarer slow path, with the compiler emitting a **deoptimization/materialization point** that reconstructs the real heap object on-demand only if the slow path is actually taken at runtime. This lets JITs capture the benefit of escape analysis even for conditionally-escaping objects, at the cost of needing a deoptimization/OSR (on-stack replacement) mechanism to materialize the object lazily.

## 6. Loop Vectorization

**SLP (superword-level parallelism) vectorization.** Operates bottom-up over straight-line code, identifying groups of **isomorphic independent scalar operations** (e.g. four separate scalar additions computing adjacent array elements) and packing them into a single SIMD operation; it builds candidate packs from adjacent memory accesses, extends packs through the use-def chains following producers/consumers, and inserts pack/unpack (shuffle) instructions at pack boundaries. Unlike loop-level vectorization, SLP doesn't require an iteration-space abstraction at all — it works equally well on manually unrolled code or straight-line basic blocks, which is why it's run as a complementary pass alongside loop vectorization in LLVM and GCC.

**Loop-level vectorization with dependence analysis.** Determines vectorization legality by computing **dependence distance and direction vectors** between array accesses across loop iterations (e.g. via the GCD test or Banerjee's test) — a dependence with distance 0 or a backward direction within the vectorized iteration group forbids vectorizing across that boundary (a true loop-carried dependence), while a sufficiently large positive distance is safe. Profitability modeling then weighs estimated vector-register-width speedup against the cost of any necessary scalar fixup code (e.g. for a trip count not divisible by the vector width), typically expressed as a target-specific cost model over the IR.

**Strip-mining, peeling, and the legality/profitability split.** **Strip-mining** transforms a loop with trip count N into an outer loop over N/VF chunks and an inner loop (or single vector operation) over the vector factor VF, which is the standard structural transform underlying vectorization. **Loop peeling** strips off a prologue (and/or epilogue) of iterations to align memory accesses to vector-width boundaries or to handle the non-multiple remainder, trading a small amount of code duplication for removing the need for masked/unaligned vector accesses in the main body.

**If-conversion and predication.** To vectorize a loop containing a conditional (`if` inside the loop body), if-conversion transforms control flow into data flow — replacing the conditional store/compute with a **select** (ternary) or a predicated/masked vector instruction (using a vector mask computed from the condition) — so that all lanes execute uniformly and only the masked lanes' results are committed. This is essential for vectorizing loops with divergent control flow and is the software analogue of hardware predication in SIMD/GPU ISAs.

**Reduction and induction variable recognition.** A loop accumulating into a scalar (`sum += a[i]`) is not trivially vectorizable because each iteration depends on the previous; the compiler must recognize this as a **reduction pattern**, vectorize it using a vector accumulator plus a final horizontal reduction (shuffle-and-add tree) after the loop, and separately recognize **induction variables** (loop counters and derived linear expressions) so that per-lane index values can be computed directly (e.g. `i, i+1, i+2, i+3` via a vector increment) rather than serially incrementing.

## 7. Instruction Scheduling

**List scheduling over a dependence DAG.** Builds a data-dependence graph per basic block (nodes are instructions, edges are true/anti/output dependences with associated latencies), then greedily selects, at each cycle, a ready instruction (all predecessors scheduled, resources available) by priority — most commonly the **critical-path heuristic**, prioritizing instructions on the longest latency-weighted path to the DAG's exit, since delaying them delays everything downstream. This is the workhorse scheduler in nearly every production backend's basic-block scheduling pass.

**Trace and superblock/hyperblock scheduling.** Basic-block scheduling can't move instructions across branches, so **global scheduling** techniques extend the scope: trace scheduling selects a likely hot linear path through multiple basic blocks (using profile data) and schedules across it as if it were one block, inserting compensation code in off-trace paths to preserve correctness when control flow diverges from the predicted trace. **Superblock scheduling** restricts this to single-entry, multiple-exit regions formed by tail-duplicating to remove side entrances, simplifying the compensation-code problem; **hyperblock scheduling** further allows multiple-entry regions by using if-conversion/predication to merge divergent paths into one predicated block before scheduling.

**Software pipelining / modulo scheduling.** For loops, rather than scheduling one iteration body, modulo scheduling overlaps successive iterations in a steady-state pattern: it computes the **Minimum Initiation Interval (MII)** as the maximum of the **ResMII** (resource-constrained bound, from functional-unit throughput) and **RecMII** (recurrence-constrained bound, from the longest latency cycle in the dependence graph, e.g. a loop-carried accumulator chain), then iteratively tries scheduling at increasing candidate initiation intervals starting at MII, backtracking on resource conflicts, until a valid modulo schedule is found. The result is explicit **prologue/steady-state kernel/epilogue** code implementing the overlapped pipeline — a technique central to VLIW and EPIC (e.g. Itanium) compilers where the hardware has no out-of-order engine to extract this overlap dynamically.

**Phase ordering with register allocation.** Scheduling before allocation can produce a schedule that requires more simultaneously-live values than there are physical registers, forcing the allocator to insert spills that invalidate the carefully chosen schedule; allocating before scheduling can introduce false dependences (anti/output dependences on reused physical registers) that constrain the scheduler unnecessarily. Production compilers typically schedule twice (an initial pre-allocation pass to expose parallelism, then a post-allocation "second pass" to fix up stalls introduced by spill code), or use integrated approaches that model register pressure directly inside the list-scheduling priority function (e.g. preferring to schedule instructions that reduce live-value count when pressure is high) to approximate a joint optimum without solving the NP-hard combined problem exactly.

## 8. Loop Optimizations

**Loop-invariant code motion (LICM).** Identifies computations whose operands are all defined outside the loop (or are themselves loop-invariant) and hoists them to the loop preheader — a dedicated single-entry block inserted specifically to give LICM (and other loop passes) a safe hoisting target. Correctness requires the hoisted computation to be safe to execute unconditionally (no risk of a trap/exception that wouldn't have occurred on some iteration), or alternatively **sinking** the computation past the loop if it's invariant but only needed on exit.

**Induction variable analysis and strength reduction.** Recognizes variables that change by a constant amount each iteration (basic induction variables) and expressions that are an affine function of them (derived induction variables, e.g. an array-indexing multiply), then rewrites expensive derived computations (`i*4`) as cheap incremental updates (`t += 4` each iteration) — **strength reduction**. **Linear function test replacement** goes further by replacing the loop's exit test (originally on the original induction variable) with an equivalent test on the strength-reduced variable, so that the original induction variable can be eliminated entirely once nothing else references it.

**Loop unrolling and unroll-and-jam.** Full unrolling replaces a loop with a fixed, small, statically-known trip count by straight-line code; partial unrolling replicates the body k times with an adjusted increment and a remainder loop (or peeled epilogue) for trip counts not divisible by k, reducing branch/loop-overhead-per-element and exposing more instruction-level parallelism and SLP-vectorization opportunity. **Unroll-and-jam** unrolls an outer loop in a nested pair and then fuses ("jams") the resulting copies of the inner loop back into one, increasing reuse of values loaded in the inner loop across what were formerly separate outer iterations — a key locality transform for matrix-style nested loops.

**Loop fusion and fission/distribution.** Fusion merges two adjacent loops with the same iteration space into one, amortizing loop overhead and improving data locality (if they touch overlapping data, fused accesses reuse cache lines); it requires that fusing preserve dependences (no statement in the second loop's body can depend on a not-yet-computed value from a later iteration of the first). Fission (distribution) is the inverse — splitting one loop into several — done to isolate a vectorizable/parallelizable portion from a portion with a loop-carried dependence that blocks those transforms.

**Loop interchange and tiling/blocking.** Interchange swaps the nesting order of two loops to change which array dimension is accessed contiguously in the innermost loop, improving spatial locality (row-major vs. column-major traversal) and strengthening vectorization legality (making the stride-1 access the one addressed by consecutive vector lanes). Tiling (blocking) decomposes a loop nest's iteration space into smaller rectangular blocks sized to fit a cache level, reordering iterations so that all accesses to a block of data happen before moving to the next block, trading some loop-control overhead for dramatically reduced cache-capacity misses on large matrix/stencil-style computations.

**The polyhedral model.** Represents each statement's iteration space as an integer polyhedron (defined by the loop bounds as affine inequalities) and each statement's data accesses and dependences as affine functions over that space; optimizations (fusion, interchange, tiling, skewing) become affine transformations of the polyhedron (a schedule matrix) subject to a legality constraint that the transformed schedule respects all dependence polyhedra. This unifies what are otherwise separate, hard-to-compose ad hoc loop transformations (interchange, fusion, tiling) into a single search/optimization problem over the space of legal affine schedules, at the cost of being applicable only to loops with affine bounds and accesses (the "polyhedral-compatible" subset of real programs) — used in GCC's Graphite and LLVM's Polly.

**Loop-closed SSA (LCSSA) as an enabling canonical form.** Many of the above passes assume a canonical loop structure: a single preheader, a single latch, and — in LCSSA — every value defined inside the loop and used outside it is routed through a φ-node at the loop exit block, so that loop-external uses never need to reason about which loop-internal definition reaches them directly. This canonicalization dramatically simplifies the implementation of LICM, unrolling, and other loop passes, since they can treat "is this value used outside the loop" as a simple syntactic check on the exit-block φs rather than a general dominance/liveness query.

---

# Compiler Internals Deep-Dive: SSA Construction, Alias Analysis, and Inlining

## 1. SSA Construction

**CFRZ dominance-frontier algorithm.** Cytron, Ferrante, Rosen, Wegman, and Zadeck's classical algorithm builds SSA in two phases. First, compute the dominator tree (typically via Lengauer-Tarjan, O(E log V) or near-linear with path compression) and the dominance frontier (DF) of each basic block B: the set of blocks Y such that B dominates a predecessor of Y but does not strictly dominate Y itself. DF is computed bottom-up over the dominator tree using the recurrence DF(B) = DFlocal(B) ∪ ⋃(DFup(C) for C in children of B), where DFlocal captures successors of B not strictly dominated by B, and DFup propagates frontiers from dominator-tree children. Second, for each variable v, phi-node placement iterates: for every block B containing an assignment to v, push B onto a worklist; pop B, and for every block Y in DF(B) lacking a phi for v, insert one and add Y to the worklist (since the phi itself is a new definition). This placement is minimal in the sense that it inserts phi-nodes exactly where dominance frontiers force a merge of distinct reaching definitions — not necessarily minimal in the stricter "no dead phi" sense (see pruned SSA below). After placement, variable renaming is a single dominator-tree preorder walk, maintaining a per-variable stack of current SSA names, pushing a new name at each definition (including phi results) and popping on exit from the subtree. Overall complexity is near-linear in program size for the common case, though DF can be quadratic in pathological CFGs (motivating the DJ-graph approach below).

**Sreedhar-Gao DJ-graph construction.** Sreedhar and Gao avoid materializing dominance frontiers explicitly, which can be large (O(V²) edges in degenerate cases), by augmenting the dominator tree (D-edges) with join edges (J-edges) from the original CFG, forming the DJ-graph. Phi placement is driven by a notion of "iterated dominance frontier" computed via a level-based worklist traversal: starting from definition blocks, J-edges are followed to merge points, and D-edges are used to propagate necessity upward only as far as dominance level requires, using a per-block "level" (dominator-tree depth) to prune redundant visits. This yields pruned SSA directly — phi-nodes are only inserted where a live, distinct definition actually reaches — at better practical complexity than naive DF materialization, and the DJ-graph is reused for later SSA-based optimizations (e.g., sparse conditional constant propagation) since it compactly encodes both control and dominance structure.

**Braun et al. construction without dominance frontiers.** This approach builds SSA incrementally during a single abstract-interpretation-style pass over the CFG (suitable for one-pass or JIT compilers where the full CFG may not be known upfront). For each block, variable reads are resolved locally: if the block already has a local definition, use it (local value numbering); otherwise recursively query predecessors. If a block has multiple predecessors and the variable isn't yet locally defined, a phi-node is optimistically inserted, marked incomplete if some predecessors aren't yet processed (supporting construction before all CFG edges are known, i.e., for blocks under construction in a single forward pass). Once all predecessors are known, the phi operands are filled in. Critically, this can create trivial phi-nodes (all operands identical or self-referential), which are eliminated by a local phi-simplification rule: a phi with only one distinct non-self operand is replaced by that operand, with uses updated transitively (this can cascade into further simplification, resembling local value numbering over the SSA graph). The trade-off: no global dominance computation is needed, making this attractive for simpler/faster front ends, but naively reconstructing SSA per-block can be pruned automatically. Its main limitation is working best with structured, single-pass-emittable CFGs.

**Minimal/semi-pruned vs. pruned SSA, and destruction.** CFRZ's base algorithm yields minimal SSA (exactly the phis forced by the dominance frontier criterion) but not pruned SSA — some inserted phis may be dead because the underlying variable isn't actually live across the merge. Semi-pruned SSA cheaply approximates liveness using a fast pre-pass (e.g., only inserting phis for variables live across block boundaries, skipping variables only live within one block) to reduce phi count before the full DF-based pass; pruned SSA additionally performs real liveness analysis to omit phis for variables not live-out. Pruned SSA costs more upfront (needs a liveness pass) but produces smaller SSA graphs, which matters for the many SSA-based optimizations whose cost scales with the number of phi/value nodes (SCCP, GVN, PRE).

**SSA destruction.** Out-of-SSA translation must replace each phi-node with explicit copies on predecessor edges, then coalesce copies away where possible via register-allocation-style coalescing. The naive approach — inserting a copy a_i = a_j at the end of each predecessor block for operand a_j of phi — is unsound in the presence of two classic hazards. The lost-copy problem arises when a value used by a later phi operand is clobbered by an earlier copy inserted on the same edge (e.g., parallel copies a=b, b=a must execute as parallel assignment, not sequential, or the swap problem occurs: naively sequentializing a=b;b=a loses b's original value). The standard fix is to compute, per CFG edge, the full *parallel copy* implied by all phis at the target block, then sequentialize using a dependency graph over copies: nodes are the copies, edges denote "must execute before," and cycles (the swap case) are broken using a temporary register. This sequentialization is essentially the same algorithm used for parallel-move resolution in register allocation. After copy insertion, coalescing (via a copy-graph with conflict constraints from a Chaitin-Briggs-style interference graph) merges SSA names sharing a webs when it's safe, reducing the number of actual physical locations and the final copy count — the quality of coalescing has a direct, measurable effect on the number of spurious moves surviving into the regalloc phase.

## 2. Alias Analysis

**Andersen's inclusion-based points-to analysis.** Andersen's analysis computes, for every pointer-typed variable p, a points-to set pts(p) ⊆ Locations, solving a system of set-inclusion constraints generated from program statements: p = &x generates x ∈ pts(p); p = q generates pts(q) ⊆ pts(p); p = *q generates ∀a ∈ pts(q): pts(a) ⊆ pts(p); *p = q generates ∀a ∈ pts(p): pts(q) ⊆ pts(a). This is solved as a graph-reachability/fixpoint problem over an inclusion (subset) graph, worklist-propagating new points-to facts until saturation. Worst-case complexity is O(n³) in program size n (each of n² possible pairs may need up to n propagation steps), though in practice near-cubic behavior dominates on real codebases, motivated the use of BDs (binary decision diagrams) or bit-vector set representations for scalability. Andersen's is strictly more precise than Steensgaard's because subset constraints are directional and not collapsed, yielding fewer spurious aliases, at higher cost.

**Steensgaard's unification-based points-to analysis.** Instead of subset constraints, Steensgaard's analysis treats assignment as equality: whenever p and q may point to overlapping sets, their points-to representatives are unified via a union-find data structure, so all variables merged into one equivalence class share a single points-to set. This produces an almost-linear algorithm (O(n log n) with near-constant-time union-find operations, using path compression and union-by-rank) but trades precision for speed: once two pointers are unified they can never be distinguished again, even if subsequent flow would have kept their targets disjoint. This makes Steensgaard's attractive for whole-program analysis in large codebases (e.g., early LLVM/GCC alias passes) where Andersen's cubic cost is prohibitive, at the cost of coarser "may-alias" answers downstream.

**Type-based alias analysis (TBAA).** TBAA exploits a language's static type system (notably C/C++'s strict-aliasing rule) to assert that two memory accesses through incompatible pointer types cannot alias, independent of any points-to computation. Implementations build a type hierarchy / "access path" tree (e.g., LLVM's `!tbaa` metadata encodes a struct-path-aware tree where each node is a (base-type, offset, access-type) tuple), and alias queries become tree-ancestor checks: two accesses may alias only if one type is a transitive member of the other at the matching offset, or they're the same scalar type. TBAA is flow- and context-insensitive by construction but extremely cheap (near O(1) per query after the type tree is built) and composes with Andersen/Steensgaard results — most compilers intersect TBAA's answer with points-to-based may-alias results, since either analysis independently proving "no alias" is sufficient to license an optimization (e.g., load/store reordering, redundant-load elimination).

**Flow-sensitivity, field-sensitivity, and memory SSA.** Flow-insensitive analyses (as above) compute one points-to set per variable valid at all program points, which is unsound to update but cheap; flow-sensitive analysis instead computes a points-to set per program point (often via an abstract-interpretation worklist over the CFG), giving strong-update capability (replacing, not merging, pts(p) after `*p = &x` when p is a must-alias singleton) at substantially higher cost, generally O(n²) to O(n³) program points times set sizes. Field-sensitivity distinguishes struct/array fields (treating `p->f1` and `p->f2` as distinct abstract locations) versus field-insensitive analysis which collapses an entire aggregate to one location; field-sensitivity is essential for precision in object-oriented or struct-heavy code but multiplies the number of abstract locations. The must-alias vs. may-alias distinction is the key output vocabulary: must-alias licenses strong updates and value propagation across stores, while may-alias only blocks unsound reordering/elimination. Memory SSA (as in LLVM's MemorySSA) reifies this by placing an SSA-like structure over memory states — MemoryDef, MemoryUse, and MemoryPhi nodes — so that redundant-load elimination, dead-store elimination, and instruction scheduling can query "which store last defined this load's memory state" in roughly the same way value-SSA queries def-use chains, converting alias analysis's pairwise may-alias queries into a sparse, incrementally-maintainable graph structure.

## 3. Inlining

**Call-graph construction and SCC-based bottom-up processing.** Interprocedural inlining normally operates over the call graph, condensed into strongly connected components (SCCs) via Tarjan's algorithm to isolate recursive cycles. The standard order is bottom-up: process callees before callers (visiting SCCs in reverse topological order of the condensed DAG), so that by the time function F is considered for inlining into its callers, F's own body has already been fully optimized and (crucially) any inlining *into* F has already happened — meaning F's "true" cost/size reflects post-inlining shrinkage from constant folding and dead-code elimination, not just its as-written size. This ordering interacts directly with other interprocedural passes (interprocedural constant propagation, argument promotion) which also prefer bottom-up or alternating fixpoint schedules. Top-down inlining (inline at a call site using the caller's as-yet-unoptimized context) is cheaper to schedule but risks inlining bloated, unoptimized callee bodies and missing simplification opportunities; most production compilers (LLVM, GCC) default to bottom-up with an outer fixpoint loop to handle newly-exposed call sites after inlining changes a caller's body.

**Cost-benefit heuristic models.** LLVM's inline cost model computes an approximate instruction-count "cost" for the callee body (weighting calls, loads/stores, branches differently, with special discounts for loop-invariant or likely-foldable operations) and compares it against a threshold modulated by call-site context: the model does a simplified abstract interpretation of the callee with actual argument values substituted where statically known, counting how many instructions would be constant-folded or branches resolved (its "bonus" terms) — this is a cheap simulation of the simplification that inlining would actually trigger, not a static size diff. The final decision is `cost < threshold`, where the threshold itself is adjusted upward for call sites inside loops, for callees marked `inline`/`__forceinline`, for single-call-site (last-call-to-static) opportunities, and downward for cold paths identified via profile data (PGO) — making the heuristic a multi-factor scoring function rather than a single size comparison. The key trade-off is code growth versus removed call overhead and unlocked downstream optimization; overly aggressive thresholds cause instruction-cache pressure and compile-time blowup, while overly conservative ones leave constant propagation and escape analysis opportunities on the table (see below).

**Recursive inlining limits and partial inlining.** Direct or mutual recursion in an SCC cannot be inlined to a fixpoint (infinite unrolling), so compilers bound recursive inlining with an explicit depth/count limit — e.g., allowing one or two levels of self-inlining to expose a common fast path (such as a base-case check) while refusing further unrolling, often gated by a separate, stricter cost threshold than non-recursive inlining. Partial inlining addresses functions with a cheap, frequently-executed fragment (e.g., a fast-path check before a rarely-taken slow path): rather than inlining the whole body, the compiler outlines the cold portion into a separate function and inlines only the hot fragment plus a call to the outlined remainder, controlled by block-frequency/profile data to identify which region is "cold." This captures most of the call-overhead benefit for the common path without the code-size cost of fully duplicating rarely-executed code.

**Speculative devirtualization combined with inlining.** For virtual/indirect calls where profiling or class-hierarchy analysis (CHA) suggests a dominant target, the compiler inserts a guarded, speculative direct call: a runtime type/vtable check comparing the actual receiver type against the predicted one, with a fast path that calls (and can then inline) the predicted target directly, and a slow path falling back to the original indirect call. This matters because indirect calls are normally opaque to the inliner (no fixed callee to analyze), so devirtualization is a prerequisite transformation that *creates* inlinable call sites; the combined transform's profitability depends on the guard's prediction accuracy (from profile data) outweighing the branch/check overhead, and it typically only triggers under PGO or strong CHA guarantees (e.g., final classes, sealed hierarchies) to avoid pessimizing correctly-behaved polymorphic code.

**Interaction with constant propagation and escape analysis.** Inlining's most significant second-order effect is exposing optimization opportunities invisible at the call-site boundary: once a callee body is substituted with its actual argument expressions, sparse conditional constant propagation can fold branches that depended on now-known-constant parameters, dead-code elimination removes now-unreachable paths, and — critically for managed/GC'd languages — escape analysis can determine that an object passed into the (now-inlined) callee never escapes the combined caller-callee scope, enabling stack allocation or scalar replacement of an otherwise heap-allocated object. This is precisely why cost models include a "simplification bonus" for constant arguments: the measured benefit of inlining is not just saved call overhead but the cascade of enabled passes, which is why inlining is typically scheduled early and iterated with cleanup passes (SCCP, DCE, GVN) rather than run once as an isolated phase.

# Register Allocation and Instruction Scheduling

## 1. Register Allocation

### 1.1 Graph-Coloring Register Allocation (Chaitin-Briggs)

The dominant classical approach models register allocation as graph coloring. After generating code with virtual registers, the compiler computes **live ranges** (via liveness analysis, a backward dataflow problem: `LiveOut[B] = ∪ LiveIn[S]` for successors S, `LiveIn[B] = Use[B] ∪ (LiveOut[B] - Def[B])`). Each live range becomes a node in an **interference graph**: an edge connects two live ranges if they are simultaneously live at some program point and thus cannot share a physical register. Building this graph naively is O(n²) in the number of variables but is typically done incrementally during a backward walk over each basic block, inserting edges between the current live set and each newly defined variable.

Chaitin's original algorithm (1981) proceeds iteratively:

1. **Build** the interference graph.
2. **Simplify**: repeatedly remove any node with degree < k (k = number of available physical registers) and push it onto a stack. Such a node is trivially colorable once its neighbors are colored, by pigeonhole.
3. **Spill decision**: if no node has degree < k, pick a node to mark for spilling using a cost heuristic, remove it from the graph (optimistically treating it as spilled), and continue simplifying.
4. **Select**: pop nodes off the stack, assigning each the first color not used by its already-colored neighbors.
5. If a node marked for spill cannot actually find a free color during select, it is actually spilled: insert store-after-def and load-before-use code, then rebuild and repeat the whole process.

**Briggs' optimistic coloring** (Briggs, Cooper, Torczon, 1994) changes step 3: nodes with degree ≥ k are *not* immediately committed to spilling. They're still pushed onto the stack (optimistically assuming a color will be available), and the actual spill/no-spill decision is deferred to the select phase. This matters because a high-degree node's neighbors may end up colored with overlapping colors, leaving a free color for it anyway — Chaitin's algorithm pessimistically spills such nodes even when unnecessary, whereas Briggs' approach only spills when select actually fails to find a color. This significantly reduces spill counts in practice without changing asymptotic complexity (still bounded by the number of build/simplify/spill iterations, each O(E) for simplify with a bucket-queue by degree).

### 1.2 Spill Cost Estimation

When simplify stalls, the heuristic for *which* node to mark for potential spill is critical. The standard Chaitin-Briggs heuristic computes a cost-to-degree ratio: `cost(v) / degree(v)`, where `cost(v)` estimates the dynamic execution cost of spilling v — typically `Σ (10^depth) over each def/use`, weighting uses inside loops exponentially higher (since spill code there executes more often), minus a bonus if v's live range crosses a call (favoring caller-saved vs callee-saved considerations). The degree term in the denominator biases toward spilling high-degree nodes, since spilling one high-degree node resolves many potential conflicts at once, maximizing the chance that simplify can proceed. Infinite-cost nodes (e.g., values defined and used within a single instruction, or pre-colored nodes for calling convention registers) are never selected.

### 1.3 Coalescing: Conservative Coalescing and Iterated Register Coalescing (IRC)

Coalescing merges two live ranges connected by a **move instruction** (copy) into a single node, eliminating the move if the merged node can still be colored — important because SSA-destruction and phi-elimination produce many copies that pure allocation would otherwise leave as real `mov` instructions. Naive coalescing can be dangerous: merging two nodes unions their neighbor sets, potentially creating a node whose degree exceeds k and forcing spills that wouldn't otherwise occur.

**Briggs' conservative coalescing** only merges nodes a and b if the resulting merged node has fewer than k neighbors of degree ≥ k (i.e., the count of "high-degree" neighbors after union is < k). This guarantees simplify can still proceed past the merged node.

**George and Appel's Iterated Register Coalescing (IRC)** interleaves coalescing with simplify/spill rather than doing it as a separate pre-pass. The worklist algorithm maintains several node categories (simplify-worklist, freeze-worklist, spill-worklist, coalesced, colored) and a move classification (coalesced, constrained, frozen, worklist, active moves). It alternates: simplify low-degree non-move-related nodes, then attempt conservative coalescing on worklist moves (using either Briggs' heuristic or **George's heuristic**, which requires that every high-degree neighbor of a already interferes with b), then "freeze" moves that can't be coalesced yet (treating them as non-move-related to unblock simplification), and finally select nodes for spilling if stuck. This tight interleaving recovers more coalescing opportunities than a strict pre-pass/post-pass separation and is the basis of allocators in LLVM's early greedy allocator ancestry and many textbook (Appel's "Modern Compiler Implementation") reference implementations.

### 1.4 Linear Scan Register Allocation

Linear scan (Poletto and Sarkar, 1999) trades optimality for speed, targeting JIT compilers where allocation time is on the critical path. It first computes **live intervals**: for each virtual register, a contiguous (or interval-list, for lifetime holes) range `[start, end]` over a linearized instruction numbering, typically derived from a linear-order traversal (not full interference graph construction). The core algorithm sorts intervals by start point and scans left to right maintaining an **active set** of intervals currently holding a physical register, sorted by end point. For each new interval: expire intervals from active whose end point precedes the new interval's start (freeing their registers); if free registers remain, assign one; otherwise, select the active interval with the *furthest end point* to spill (a greedy heuristic minimizing wasted register occupancy), spilling either it or the new interval depending on which frees a register for the longer-lived value. This is O(n log n) overall (dominated by sorting), vastly cheaper than graph coloring's iterative rebuild cycles, at the cost of generating more spill code than Chaitin-Briggs in register-constrained code — an accepted trade-off for JIT warm-up latency (used historically in HotSpot's client compiler and early JIT designs). Second-chance / lazy binding allocators used in trace-based or baseline JITs extend this further: they defer or "lazily" re-materialize bindings at block boundaries, avoiding global interval computation entirely and instead patching allocation decisions incrementally as new traces are compiled, trading allocation quality for near-zero compile-time overhead.

### 1.5 SSA-Based Register Allocation

A key theoretical result (Hack, Grund, Goos; Brisk et al.) is that the interference graph of a program in strict SSA form is a **chordal graph**, and chordal graphs are colorable in polynomial time optimally via a **perfect elimination ordering** (obtainable via maximum cardinality search), without the heuristic simplify/spill guessing needed for general graphs. This enables "SSA-based coloring": color greedily in elimination order, and because of chordality, simplify never gets stuck below k if the register pressure (computed exactly via max live-range overlap at any program point) doesn't exceed k. Spilling is instead handled *before* coloring via explicit pressure-reduction passes, and coalescing becomes a **puzzle-solving problem** — because SSA keeps per-definition values distinct, merging phi-related copies at block boundaries requires solving register-shuffling "permutation puzzles" at control-flow joins, solved via cyclic permutation decomposition into swaps/moves, rather than the move-coalescing graph surgery of non-SSA allocators.

## 2. Instruction Scheduling

### 2.1 List Scheduling

The workhorse local scheduling algorithm operates over a **data-dependence DAG** built per basic block: nodes are instructions, edges represent true (RAW), anti (WAR), output (WAW) dependencies, and edge weights encode latency. **Priority-based list scheduling** maintains a ready list of instructions whose predecessors have already been scheduled, and at each cycle selects the highest-priority ready instruction to issue, subject to resource constraints (functional unit availability, modeled via a reservation-table or resource-vector simulating pipeline occupancy). The classic priority function is the **critical-path (longest-path) heuristic**: priority(n) = length of the longest latency-weighted path from n to any DAG leaf. This is computed via a single reverse topological pass, O(V+E), and favors instructions on the schedule's critical path to avoid stalling later work — minimizing the makespan under a greedy, generally NP-hard scheduling problem (list scheduling is a heuristic approximation, not optimal, though it achieves known approximation bounds for certain machine models). Ties are typically broken by number of successors or register-pressure impact.

### 2.2 Local vs. Global Scheduling: Trace Scheduling

Basic-block (local) scheduling is limited by block boundaries, missing cross-block parallelism. **Trace scheduling** (Fisher) extends scheduling across block boundaries by selecting a likely execution path (a "trace") through multiple basic blocks — using profile data or heuristics to pick the hot path — and scheduling instructions across the trace as if it were one large block. Instructions can move above/below branches that aren't part of the trace, requiring **compensation code**: bookkeeping copies inserted off-trace to preserve correctness when control flow exits the trace early or enters it mid-way (join points) — e.g., an instruction speculatively hoisted above a branch must be replicated on the off-trace path if it was skipped there. This compensation code is a major complexity and correctness burden, and its potential code-size blowup is the central trade-off vs. simpler block-local scheduling. **Superblock scheduling** simplifies this by applying tail duplication to eliminate side-entrances into the trace (so only the top of a superblock has multiple entries), reducing compensation code needs at the cost of code duplication; **hyperblock scheduling** further merges predicated/if-converted control flow into a single block to expose more ILP, trading branch overhead for predicate-execution overhead on architectures supporting predication.

### 2.3 Software Pipelining and Modulo Scheduling

For loops, basic-block-local ILP is often insufficient; **software pipelining** overlaps iterations so that different pipeline stages of consecutive iterations execute concurrently, exposing a steady-state loop body (the "kernel") preceded by a prologue and followed by an epilogue that ramp in/out of the overlapped execution. **Modulo scheduling** is the standard formalization: it schedules one iteration's instructions into a fixed-length repeating pattern with period **II (initiation interval)**, the number of cycles between the start of successive iterations. The II is bounded below by the **MII (minimum initiation interval)** = max(ResMII, RecMII): **ResMII** is the resource-constrained lower bound (ceiling of max over all resource types of demand/availability), and **RecMII** is the recurrence-constrained lower bound derived from the longest latency-weighted cycle in the dependence graph divided by its distance (iteration-carried dependence cycles, e.g., loop-carried accumulator chains, impose a minimum period). **Iterative modulo scheduling** (Rau) starts at II = MII and attempts to schedule all operations into a **modulo reservation table** (a resource-conflict table of size II that wraps cyclically); on failure (resource conflict or dependence violation) it backtracks/reschedules offending instructions, and if scheduling repeatedly fails it increments II and retries — this is heuristic, not guaranteed polynomial, but converges quickly in practice for typical loop bodies. This matters enormously for VLIW/EPIC architectures (e.g., Itanium) where the compiler, not hardware, is solely responsible for exposing multiple-issue parallelism; the absence of dynamic out-of-order scheduling hardware makes static modulo scheduling essential for achieving throughput on tight numerical loops.

### 2.4 VLIW/EPIC Scheduling and the Register-Allocation Interaction

VLIW/EPIC scheduling must jointly pack multiple independent operations into each issue bundle, respecting both the dependence DAG and the explicit, statically-known resource template (which functional-unit slots exist per bundle) — unlike superscalar list scheduling, there's no hardware scoreboard to rescue a bad static schedule. This exacerbates the classic **phase-ordering problem** between scheduling and register allocation: scheduling-before-allocation maximizes ILP by freely reordering and widening the live ranges of virtual registers to fill slots, but this increases register pressure, potentially forcing a subsequent allocator to spill, which reintroduces serializing memory operations that invalidate the carefully built schedule. Allocation-before-scheduling instead fixes physical registers first, which can introduce false WAR/WAW dependencies between unrelated operations assigned the same physical register, limiting the scheduler's reordering freedom. Practical compilers use **integrated** or iterative approaches: scheduling with a register-pressure-sensitive priority function (penalizing moves that would extend live ranges past the available register count), interleaved passes of scheduling and allocation (schedule, then allocate, then reschedule around inserted spill code), or unified heuristics within a single pass that track both resource occupancy and register pressure simultaneously, accepting a secondary-criteria tie-break (e.g., prefer the ready instruction that shortens the most live ranges) when multiple instructions are equally ready on the critical path.

# Compiler Optimization Mechanisms: Escape Analysis, Loop Vectorization, and Loop Transformations

## 1. Escape Analysis

Escape analysis determines whether an object's lifetime or visibility can be proven to be confined to the allocating method/thread, enabling allocation-elimination and synchronization-elimination optimizations downstream.

**Connection-graph-based escape analysis (Choi-Gupta-Midkiff, HotSpot C2).** This is the canonical algorithm used in HotSpot's server compiler. It builds a *connection graph* whose nodes represent objects (allocation sites), fields, and local/global references, with edges representing "points-to" and "deferred" (reference-copy) relationships. The algorithm runs in two phases: an intraprocedural phase that builds the graph bottom-up over the method's SSA/IR nodes, propagating points-to edges through loads, stores, phi nodes, and calls; and an interprocedural phase that merges callee graphs into the caller at inlined or analyzed call sites, since escape status is not compositional without knowing how arguments are used by callees. Each node is assigned one of three escape states — `NoEscape` (object is provably local to the method and does not escape even to callees), `ArgEscape` (object escapes only as an argument to a call but not globally), and `GlobalEscape` (object escapes to the heap, a static field, or an unanalyzed call). The state is computed via a fixed-point propagation: any edge from a node to a node already marked `GlobalEscape` promotes the source, and any store of a `NoEscape` object into a field of an `ArgEscape`/`GlobalEscape` object promotes it transitively. The complexity is roughly O(N·E) for N nodes and E edges per fixed-point iteration, bounded in practice by capping interprocedural depth (HotSpot bounds connection graph growth via inlining depth and bytecode size budgets). This directly feeds scalar replacement and lock elision, discussed below; critically, it interacts with HotSpot's inliner because escape precision is gated on how much of the call graph is actually inlined — an un-inlined call conservatively marks its arguments as escaping unless annotated otherwise.

**Flow-insensitive vs. flow-sensitive escape analysis.** Flow-insensitive analysis (what the connection-graph algorithm above essentially is, in its classic form) treats the method body as an unordered set of statements, merging points-to effects without regard to program order; this is cheap (effectively a single pass over an abstracted statement set) but imprecise when escape status changes over time, e.g., an object stored into a field and later nulled out. Flow-sensitive escape analysis instead tracks escape state per program point via a dataflow framework over the control-flow graph (a forward dataflow problem with a lattice of escape states and a meet operator that is the "most conservative" state at control-flow merges). Flow sensitivity gives strictly more precision — it can recognize that an object escapes only on one control path and allow safe optimization on the other (e.g. partial escape analysis, below) — at the cost of iterating to a fixed point over the full CFG rather than a single structural pass, pushing complexity toward O(N·D) where D is CFG depth/iteration count under a standard worklist algorithm. Production JITs (HotSpot) use largely flow-insensitive intraprocedural analysis for cost reasons, while research/managed systems (and Graal, see below) adopt flow-sensitive formulations because the JIT's time budget is less constrained by sheer throughput demands at the method granularity they operate on.

**Scalar replacement of aggregates (SRA).** Once escape analysis proves an allocation is `NoEscape`, scalar replacement decomposes the object into its constituent fields as independent SSA scalars, eliminating the heap allocation entirely. The algorithm identifies all field accesses on the allocation node in the connection graph, replaces each `getfield`/`putfield` with direct SSA value flow (using phi nodes at control-flow merges exactly as a register promotion / mem2reg pass would), and deletes the allocation node, its initialization, and (if no synchronization survives) its monitor operations. This is essentially an extension of the mem2reg/SROA (scalar replacement of aggregates) transformation familiar from LLVM, but gated specifically on escape analysis rather than purely syntactic local-ness (SROA in LLVM alone cannot safely decompose an object whose address might leak; escape analysis is the enabling precondition). The benefit is removing allocation overhead (bump-pointer or free-list allocation, GC write-barrier avoidance, and reduced GC pressure/pause time) at the cost of potentially increasing register pressure if the aggregate has many live fields simultaneously — compilers must balance SRA against spill cost, and HotSpot bounds it by object size/field count heuristics.

**Synchronization elimination (lock elision).** If escape analysis proves an object is thread-local (not merely method-local but never published to another thread — a strictly stronger property than `NoEscape`/`ArgEscape`, sometimes tracked as a separate `NoEscape`+thread-confinement flag), any `monitorenter`/`monitorexit` pair (or `synchronized` block) operating on it can be removed, since no other thread can ever contend for that lock. This requires a *thread-escape* variant of the analysis distinguishing "escapes the method" from "escapes to another thread" — an object can escape a method (e.g., passed to a callee) yet still be provably thread-confined if the callee is also analyzed and doesn't hand it to another thread or store it where a different thread could observe it. This matters enormously for idioms like autoboxing or `StringBuffer` usage inside single-threaded hot loops, where the JIT removes lock overhead (CAS/fence costs) with zero source-level change.

**Partial escape analysis (Graal).** Classical escape analysis is all-or-nothing per allocation: one escaping path anywhere in the method poisons the whole object. Partial escape analysis (as implemented in Graal) instead performs the analysis control-flow-sensitively and allows an object to be virtualized (scalar-replaced) along paths where it does not escape, materializing it (actually allocating it) only at the specific control-flow edges where escape occurs, using Graal's EA framework integrated with its speculative/deoptimization infrastructure. This is implemented via "virtual object" nodes that track field state symbolically through the IR; at merge points where only some predecessors have a materialized object, the compiler inserts an actual allocation that reconstructs the object from the virtualized fields (a "materialization" node) only on that path, which may be moved behind a deoptimization guard if the compiler speculates the path is rarely taken. This trades a small amount of uncommon-path overhead for optimizing the dominant path fully, directly interacting with Graal's speculative deoptimization framework and its node-based sea-of-nodes IR, which makes virtual-object merging a natural extension of its existing phi/merge handling.

## 2. Loop Vectorization

**SLP (superword-level parallelism) vectorization.** SLP, originating from Larsen & Amarasinghe, targets straight-line (or lightly-structured) code containing multiple isomorphic scalar operations, rather than a single loop's repeated iterations. The algorithm builds "pack" candidates by starting from adjacent memory accesses (seed pairs, typically adjacent array stores/loads) and greedily growing packs by following def-use chains: if two isomorphic scalar instructions each produce operands that themselves are packable, they're combined into a wider "group." This proceeds via a worklist-driven pass that computes a dependence graph to verify no partial ordering is violated by packing, then schedules packed instructions together, finally emitting a single vector instruction per pack with shuffles/inserts at pack boundaries where values can't be kept purely in vector form. Complexity is roughly linear in basic block size per seed, times the number of seeds, since pack growth follows use-def chains, not full dataflow fixed-point iteration. SLP is complementary to loop vectorization proper: it captures parallelism that doesn't come from loop trip count (e.g. independent field updates on a struct, or unrolled loop bodies), and most production vectorizers (LLVM's SLPVectorizer, HotSpot C2's SuperWord pass) run it either standalone or as a follow-up to loop unrolling.

**Loop-level auto-vectorization with dependence analysis.** For a candidate loop, the vectorizer must prove it's legal to execute multiple iterations simultaneously (SIMD-width lanes), which requires dependence analysis between memory accesses across iterations. The standard formalism is distance vectors and direction vectors: for a pair of array references in nested loops, the compiler computes, per loop level, whether the dependence distance is a known constant (distance vector) or only a sign/direction (`<`, `=`, `>`, direction vector) when exact distances can't be resolved (e.g., due to symbolic bounds). Tests like the GCD test, Banerjee's inequalities, or the simpler but common "ZIV/SIV/MIV" classification (zero/single/multiple index variable tests) are applied depending on how many induction variables appear in the subscript expression. If a loop-carried true dependence exists with a distance smaller than the vectorization factor, vectorization is illegal (or requires algorithmic restructuring); anti- and output dependences can sometimes be handled by renaming. This dependence information is what gates vectorization legality and is the same machinery loop-interchange and tiling rely on, so it's typically computed once and shared across the loop-optimization pipeline.

**Vectorization legality/profitability model.** Even when legal, vectorizing is not always profitable: the compiler (e.g. LLVM's LoopVectorizer) builds a cost model comparing scalar loop cost (per-iteration instruction cost times trip count) against vectorized cost (vector instruction cost, accounting for target-specific throughput/latency tables, plus overhead for any required shuffles, gather/scatter, masking, or scalarization of unsupported operations) across a range of candidate vectorization factors (VF) and unroll factors (UF). This is often solved via an exhaustive or greedy search over a small discrete VF×UF space using target-specific `TargetTransformInfo`-style cost queries, selecting the configuration minimizing estimated cycles per element while respecting register-pressure constraints. This model's accuracy is central to avoiding "pessimization," where a legally-vectorizable loop is actually slower vectorized due to misaligned loads, cross-lane shuffle overhead, or SIMD-width underutilization from small trip counts — hence the model also factors in strip-mining/peeling overhead (below).

**Strip-mining and loop peeling for vectorization.** Strip-mining (also called loop sectioning) transforms a loop with unknown or non-multiple-of-VF trip count into an outer loop iterating over VF-sized strips and an inner fully-vectorized body, plus a scalar remainder loop (or masked final iteration) handling the tail. Peeling removes a small prefix of iterations (e.g. to align memory accesses to vector-width boundaries) to let the main vectorized body assume alignment, avoiding costly unaligned loads/stores on architectures where that matters (less critical on modern x86 with fast unaligned access, still relevant on some SIMD ISAs). Both are essential companions to the legality/profitability analysis since they convert "approximately vectorizable" loops into provably-correct vector code plus a cheap scalar fixup.

**If-conversion/predication and reduction/induction recognition.** If-conversion transforms control flow inside a loop body (conditional branches) into straight-line code using select/mask operations (predicated execution), which is necessary because SIMD lanes execute in lockstep and can't naturally diverge; on architectures with mask registers (AVX-512, SVE) this maps directly to predicated vector instructions, while on others it requires blend/select sequences, trading control-flow overhead for potentially wasted lane work. Reduction recognition identifies accumulation patterns (`sum += a[i]`) and induction-variable recognition identifies affine index variables, both essential because a naive vectorizer would see a loop-carried dependence on `sum` and declare the loop unvectorizable; instead, the compiler recognizes the *reduction idiom*, vectorizes partial sums into a vector accumulator, and emits a horizontal reduction (shuffle-and-add tree) at the end, while induction variables are rewritten so each lane computes its own offset affinely rather than serially incrementing.

## 3. General Loop Optimizations

**Loop-invariant code motion (LICM).** LICM identifies computations inside a loop body whose operands are all defined outside the loop (or are themselves loop-invariant), and hoists them to the loop preheader — a dedicated single-entry block inserted before the loop header, which is part of the canonical loop form requirement. The algorithm typically works over loop-nest structure (identified via dominator-tree-based natural loop detection) combined with reaching-definitions or SSA use-def chains: an instruction is invariant if all its operands are either constants, defined outside the loop, or themselves already-hoisted invariant instructions, computed via a fixed-point pass over the loop body in a single traversal order respecting dominance. Correctness requires the hoisted instruction to be safe to execute unconditionally (no side effects, or if it has side effects/may trap, speculation is only allowed when the compiler can prove it always executes, e.g. dominates all loop exits). LICM is foundational and runs iteratively interleaved with other passes (GVN, unrolling) since each transformation can expose new invariant code.

**Induction variable analysis and strength reduction / linear function test replacement.** The compiler canonicalizes all induction variables (IVs) into a basis of one or more "basic" IVs plus derived IVs expressed as affine functions of the basic one (`j = a*i + b`), typically via LLVM's `IndVarSimplify`/SCEV (scalar evolution) analysis, which represents each value as a closed-form recurrence (`{start, +, step}` in SCEV notation). Strength reduction then rewrites expensive derived computations (e.g., array address calculations involving multiplication) as a running sum updated by addition each iteration (`addr += stride` rather than `addr = base + i*stride`), eliminating multiplications inside the loop at the cost of maintaining one extra live induction variable per rewritten expression. Linear function test replacement (LFTR) goes further by rewriting the loop's exit test to use one of the strength-reduced IVs instead of the original counter, so that once all original uses of `i` are gone, `i` itself can be eliminated entirely — this matters because naive strength reduction alone leaves both the original counter (for the comparison) and the new IV alive, doubling IV overhead; LFTR removes that redundancy.

**Loop unrolling (full vs. partial) and unroll-and-jam.** Full unrolling replicates the entire loop body for every iteration when the trip count is a known small constant, eliminating branch and induction-update overhead entirely at the cost of code size. Partial unrolling replicates the body U times, adjusting the induction step, and leaves a (possibly peeled/strip-mined) remainder loop, chosen to expose more independent instruction-level parallelism and amortize branch overhead while bounding code growth. Unroll-and-jam is the combination of unrolling an outer loop in a nest and then fusing ("jamming") the resulting copies of the inner loop together, which increases reuse of loop-invariant loads/data across the fused inner bodies and increases register-level parallelism — this is a classic locality-and-ILP optimization distinct from plain unrolling since it operates across loop-nest levels and requires legality checks akin to loop fusion (no dependence violated by interleaving statements from different original outer iterations).

**Loop fusion/fission, interchange, and tiling.** Fusion merges two adjacent loops with compatible iteration spaces into one to improve data locality (shared cache lines touched once) and reduce loop overhead, legal only when no dependence from the second loop's body to the first (after fusion) would reverse original execution order. Fission (distribution) is the inverse — splitting one loop into several — often used to isolate a vectorizable portion from a non-vectorizable one, or to reduce register pressure/working set per loop. Loop interchange swaps the nesting order of two loops in a perfectly (or imperfectly, with extra legality care) nested loop to change the stride pattern of the innermost loop's memory accesses, converting a column-major stride-N access into a row-major stride-1 access for substantially better cache-line utilization and prefetcher behavior; legality again rests on direction-vector analysis — interchange is illegal if it would reverse a dependence direction. Loop tiling (blocking) partitions iteration space into smaller rectangular blocks sized to fit a cache level, restructuring a loop nest into an outer "tile loop" iterating over blocks and an inner loop iterating within a block, trading a more complex control structure for dramatically improved reuse in cache-sensitive kernels like matrix multiplication; tile size selection is itself a profitability/cost-model problem tied to target cache geometry.

**Polyhedral model and canonical/loop-closed SSA forms.** The polyhedral model represents affine loop nests (bounds and array subscripts all affine functions of enclosing loop indices and symbolic parameters) as integer polyhedra, with iteration order encoded via a scheduling function; legal transformations (fusion, interchange, tiling, skewing) become affine transformations of these polyhedra validated by polyhedral dependence analysis (e.g. via the Omega test or integer linear programming feasibility), enabling a single unified search over a much larger transformation space than ad hoc pairwise legality checks — this is the basis of tools/passes like Polly (LLVM) and underlies much of GCC's Graphite. All of these transformations depend on the compiler maintaining canonical loop forms: a single preheader, a single latch, identified exit blocks, and loop-closed SSA form (where every value used outside the loop is routed through a phi node in a dedicated exit block, ensuring no loop-internal SSA value has uses outside the loop directly) — this canonicalization is what lets LICM, unrolling, interchange, and fusion passes reason locally about a loop's boundary without re-deriving control-flow structure each time, and it's why loop-simplify/LCSSA-style passes run as prerequisites before the optimization passes proper.
